The unconditional-copy and copyable-vacancy regime was not found in the literature. This may explain the atypical fingerprint, but that is untested. full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** I'm changing the first pass's KNOWN-VARIANT to KNOWN. The behaviour is mostly multi-state voter-model coarsening with some noise added. The "Schelling segregation" part is largely a labelling artifact, not a separate route to segregation.

**Why the first pass's framing doesn't hold**
- The documented Schelling–Voter hybrid works differently. There, an unhappy agent is selected at random, and she chooses to play one of two different games: either she migrates to another place where she will be happy (with probability p), or she changes her own type (with probability 1−p). In this system, every cell copies a random neighbour every step, whether or not it is unhappy.
- That makes rule (2), applied to all cells including empty ones, a synchronous voter model with three states, where "empty" is one of the states. This is my reading of the rule text, not something I measured. If it's right, vacancies are not conserved, so the vacancy mechanism behind Schelling coarsening doesn't apply as such.
- The copying rule is strong enough to swamp the move rule. That explains why 33 rule programs with thresholds from 0.2 to 0.4, either rule order and 3–4 types all give the same fingerprint. The threshold and the order barely matter.

**Why the observed fingerprint matches voter coarsening**
- The 2D voter model is a known marginal case. It coarsens through interfacial noise, not curvature. It is characterized by a slow, logarithmic decay of the density of interfaces ρ∼1/ln t (as opposed to the algebraic decay ρ∼1/L(t)∼t^(-1/z) of curvature-driven growth). It also produces patterns with clusters of all sizes between 1 and √t.
- That fits what was seen: about 6 domains, a short correlation length (about 2.3), all 3 types still present at high entropy, and frequent reversals (flickering at interfaces). On a 64×64 grid, voter coarsening hasn't finished by the end of a finite run. The Schelling moves just add noise on top.
- This also explains why it "passes the coarsening test but doesn't look like a textbook case." Schelling-type coarsening shows algebraic growth. For example, one study finds the interface density decays as a power law with an exponent α≃0.5 for the limit of small vacancy density. Voter coarsening is logarithmic and tensionless, so it looks different.
- Related variants that I did not check against this run:
  - Adding intermediate states can restore an effective surface tension.
  - Even a small number of Ising-type agents can switch the dynamics to curvature-driven growth. Even a very small (∼1%) fraction of Ising agents changes the tensionless dynamics into the curvature-driven Ising-like dynamics.
  - Schelling moves acting as noise sit within this known family of perturbed voter models.

**Genuine pattern or artifact?** The coarsening itself is real but generic: plain voter-model ordering that was still incomplete when the run stopped. Calling it "segregation with vacancies" is an artifact of how the rules are described. Updating every cell at once may increase the reversal count. I'm not aware of any feature here that a multi-state synchronous voter model with added noise wouldn't reproduce.

**What would change my verdict:** If interface density over time decays algebraically rather than as 1/ln t, or if the vacancy fraction stays constant (meaning empty cells aren't actually copied), I'd move to KNOWN-VARIANT. It would then be Schelling-driven coarsening with voter noise, closer to the hybrid model above. A t-vs-ρ log-plot would settle it.
